raw_case_text:
A 74-year-old woman, living in Tunis, Tunisia, was admitted for an investigation of fever evolving since weeks accompanied by sweating and chills. Oral temperature ranging from 38 to 39 C had been regularly measured. She also complained of fatigue, diarrhea, unclear abdominal pain and occasional non-productive cough. Her sole medical history was a well-controlled hypertension. Physical examination was poor, revealing a palpable spleen just below the left costal margin after deep inspiration. A well-circumscribed, erythematous plaque with a thin rolled border and large erosions and crusts on the surface A single well-defined, ulcer surrounded by erythematous edging, with serous oozing (3x3cm in size), was observed at her right arm near the axilla (Figure 1 A). The patient reported that the lesion was painless without tendency to heal, but could not precisely recall when it had first appeared (2 or 3 years). The rest of the physical examination was essentially normal. Otherwise, the patient presented neither risk factors of HIV infection nor chronic disease, transfusion or immunosuppressive therapy. Laboratory findings on admission demonstrated in the blood count a pancytopenia with normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin of 8.7 g/dL), leucocytopenia (2900/mm3) and thrombocytopenia (113000/mm3). Sedimentation rate was 115mm (1st hour), C-reactive protein 215mg/l and procalcitonine <0.5 ng/ml. Serum Protein Electrophoresis displayed an abnormal pattern with a hypoalbuminemia at 31.1 g/l and a monoclonal hypergammaglobulinemia at 38.4 g/l. Her renal, liver and hemostasis function tests were normal. Chest imaging and cardiac ultrasounds were within normal limits. However, abdomino-pelvic imaging (ultrasound and scan) revealed the presence of a homogenous hepatosplenomegaly. Initially differential diagnosis mainly included brucellosis, typhoid fever, visceral leishmaniasis and hematological malignancies. Bacteriological cultures of blood (3 series), stool and urine revealed all negative. Hepatitis B Virus, Salmonella and Brucella antibody tests were also unrevealing. However, Leishmania rk39 immuno-chromatography test was positive, consistent with a VL diagnosis. A bone marrow aspiration was performed. Its parasitological examination revealed the presence of Leishmania amastigote forms. The patient serum was also positive for Leishmania anti-bodies by immunofluorescence antibody test (titer = 1/400). Blood parasite load determined by a real time quantitative PCR (qPCR) targeting the Leishmania kinetoplast was 400 parasites/ml.
On another hand, direct microscopic examination performed on skin smears showed no Leishmania amastigotes. However, Leishmania DNA amplification was obtained from the dermal DNA extract, using the same qPCR. Molecular typing of isolates obtained from both samples (blood and skin) was carried out by sequence analysis of ribosomal internal transcribed spacer 1 (ITS1) region of rRNA gene. This analysis showed that the Leishmania strains from the arm cutaneous lesion and the blood corresponded to the species L. infantum and were 100% identical. Visceral Leishmaniasis diagnosis was retained and a course of anti-leishmanial therapy with intravenous amphotericin B deoxycholate at a dose of 1 g/kg/day every 2 days was started. The patient developed a mild renal failure, which was corrected after spacing the cures and rehydration. The response to treatment was rapidly favorable with apyrexia and an improvement in general conditions including resolution of fatigue and increased appetite. The splenomegaly resolved and blood count levels returned to reference ranges. Real-time PCR in blood after 28 days of treatment revealed negative. However, the skin lesion did not improve although Leishmania qPCR on dermal sample became negative. The physician reconsidered CL diagnosis and recommended a skin biopsy which was refused by the patient. A year later, the lesion was clinically almost the same (Figure 1 B). A polarized dermoscopy examination revealed ulcerations and short, fine arborizing vessels (Figure 2), evocative of a basal cell carcinoma. Histopathology examination of the skin lesion biopsy, finally accepted by the patient, confirmed the diagnosis of basal cell carcinoma. A complete excision of the tumor was performed and the evolution was good.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 74-year-old female presented with weeks of persistent fever with chills and sweats, accompanied by fatigue, diarrhea, vague abdominal pain, and a chronic non-healing ulcer on her right arm.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with several weeks of persistent fever (regularly measuring 38 to 39 C orally) accompanied by chills, drenching sweats, fatigue, diarrhea, unclear abdominal pain, and an occasional non-productive cough. She also reported a painless ulcer on her right upper arm near the axilla that had failed to heal over the preceding 2 to 3 years. She was admitted for inpatient investigation of fever of unknown origin.
subjective.past_medical_history: Well-controlled essential hypertension. No history of HIV risk factors, chronic immunosuppression, or blood transfusions. Epidemiological exposure: resident of Tunis, Tunisia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Fatigue, watery diarrhea, vague abdominal discomfort, non-productive cough, chills, sweats. Home medications: antihypertensive therapy. Allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: General: oral temperature 38 to 39 C. Abdomen: palpable spleen tip just below the left costal margin on deep inspiration. Dermatologic: a single well-defined, ulcerated plaque surrounded by an erythematous border with serous oozing (3 x 3 cm in size) on the right upper arm near the axilla. Rest of the physical examination was normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Hematology: Hemoglobin: 8.7 g/dL (normocytic normochromic anemia); Leukocyte count: 2,900/mm3; Platelet count: 113,000/mm3 (pancytopenia). Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 115 mm/1st hour; C-reactive protein: 215 mg/L; Procalcitonin: <0.5 ng/mL. Serum protein electrophoresis: albumin 31.1 g/L, monoclonal hypergammaglobulinemia 38.4 g/L. Renal, liver, and coagulation tests: normal. Chest radiography and transthoracic echocardiography: normal. Abdominopelvic ultrasonography and CT: homogenous hepatosplenomegaly. Blood cultures (3 sets), stool cultures, and urine cultures: all negative. Serologies for Hepatitis B, Salmonella, and Brucella: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow aspiration: performed for cytological and parasitological examination. Skin smear microscopy from arm lesion: direct microscopic examination negative for fungal elements and amastigotes. Polarized dermoscopy of the right arm ulcer: ulceration with short, fine arborizing telangiectatic vessels evocative of basal cell carcinoma. Histopathological examination of right arm skin biopsy: confirmed basal cell carcinoma.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Visceral leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania infantum, co-occurring with an independent cutaneous basal cell carcinoma of the right arm.
Diagnostic confirmation: Leishmania rK39 immunochromatographic test was positive; bone marrow aspirate parasitological examination demonstrated Leishmania amastigote forms; indirect immunofluorescence antibody test (IFAT) titer was positive at 1:400; real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) targeting the Leishmania kinetoplast demonstrated a blood parasite load of 400 parasites/mL. Molecular typing of isolates from both blood and dermal DNA by internal transcribed spacer 1 (ITS1) rRNA gene sequencing confirmed 100% identity to Leishmania infantum. Histopathology of the skin biopsy confirmed basal cell carcinoma.
Differentials ruled out: Brucellosis, typhoid fever, systemic bacteremia, and hematological malignancies.
Treatment and clinical course: Treated with intravenous amphotericin B deoxycholate (1 mg/kg every 2 days; paper noted 1 g/kg/day typo), with transient mild renal impairment resolving after fluid rehydration and dose spacing. Achieved complete defervescence, resolution of fatigue, resolution of splenomegaly, normalization of blood counts, and negative repeat blood qPCR at 28 days. The cutaneous basal cell carcinoma was successfully treated by complete surgical excision with clear margins.
